exam: A 2‑year‑old from a consanguineous marriage presents with chronic cough and failure to thrive – what inheritance pattern should you consider and why? — Recognise autosomal recessive pattern; link to cystic fibrosis.

You suspect sickle cell disease in a child with vaso‑occlusive pain; which test confirms the diagnosis and what does a positive result indicate? — Hemoglobin electrophoresis; presence of HbS homozygosity confirms AR sickle cell disease.
A newborn screen for PKU is unavailable; what bedside clue and simple test can you use? — Look for eczema, seizures; obtain plasma phenylalanine level; elevated level suggests AR PKU.
How would you counsel a couple who are both carriers for CF about future pregnancies? — Explain 25 % risk per pregnancy, options for prenatal diagnosis or pre‑implantation genetic testing.
What distinguishes an autosomal recessive disorder from an autosomal dominant one on a pedigree? — AR shows affected individuals in sibships with unaffected parents; AD shows vertical transmission.

In a resource‑limited hospital, genetic testing is not possible; what management steps are essential for a child with suspected AR disease? — Provide symptom‑directed therapy, preventive vaccinations, nutritional support, and arrange referral for possible genetic counselling.
Why is hydroxyurea preferred for sickle cell disease in low‑resource settings? — Increases HbF, reduces pain crises, inexpensive, oral formulation.

A patient with confirmed CF asks about CFTR modulators; why might they be unavailable and what alternative care should you offer? — High cost and limited supply; focus on airway clearance, pancreatic enzymes, and infection control.
ai.title: Autosomal Recessive Inheritance
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Autosomal recessive inheritance requires two pathogenic alleles for disease expression. Consanguinity and carrier frequency raise risk, especially in low‑resource African settings.

b: 1/4 chance of an affected child when both parents are carriers
Carrier frequency can be high in certain Kenyan ethnic groups
sections.p: A disorder is autosomal recessive when both copies of a gene on a non‑sex chromosome are mutated. Parents are typically asymptomatic carriers.

b: Homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations required
No disease expression in heterozygotes because one normal allele supplies enough protein
sections.p: Each autosome carries two alleles; loss‑of‑function mutations on both alleles abolish normal protein activity.

b: Transcriptional up‑regulation cannot compensate for a null allele
Some carriers show mild biochemical changes but no clinical disease
sections.p: Gene expression is controlled by promoters, enhancers and epigenetic marks; recessive disease manifests when the remaining functional allele is absent, not when regulation fails.

b: Cystic fibrosis (CFTR), sickle cell disease (β‑globin), phenylketonuria (PAH) are classic examples
In low‑resource settings, malaria‑endemic regions have higher carrier rates for sickle cell
sections.p: Mutations may be missense, nonsense, splice‑site, small deletions or large rearrangements that produce non‑functional protein.

b: Ask about consanguinity, affected siblings, ethnic background
Explain 25 % recurrence risk for each pregnancy
Identify at‑risk families for targeted screening (e.g., CF, PKU, sickle cell)
sections.p: Recognising AR patterns guides counselling, carrier testing and anticipatory management, especially where newborn screening is unavailable.

t.b: Detects functional deficiency when genetic testing unavailable; abnormal result supports diagnosis

Sickle cell: hydroxyurea to raise HbF, infection prophylaxis, pain control

sections.p: Treat the disease‑specific manifestations; provide genetic counselling and preventive care.
